benchmarks.raw_results_summary: Returned 31 unique web results across 5 query variants. Results include titles, URLs, and snippets from diverse sources (Forbes, ScienceDirect, BuiltIn, etc.).
benchmarks.notes: Works reliably. DuckDuckGo HTML parsing is functional. Results are shallow (title + snippet only). No citation or provenance metadata. Query variant generation is simplistic (keyword reordering).

team_feedback.from_team2: Functional and reliable. Main weakness is shallow data — only titles and snippets, no full-text extraction. Query variants could be smarter (e.g., synonym expansion, domain-specific terms). No rate limiting between requests risks throttling on heavy use.

benchmarks.raw_results_summary: Returned 0 results. Wikipedia API returned HTTP 403 Forbidden, indicating the User-Agent or request pattern is being blocked.
benchmarks.notes: BUG: Wikipedia API returns 403 Forbidden in sandbox environments. The code structure is sound (search -> details -> see_also expansion), but the API is inaccessible. The error is silently swallowed — returns empty results with no error indication in the output metadata.

team_feedback.from_team2: Critical bug: HTTP 403 from Wikipedia API is silently swallowed, returning empty results with no error field. The method needs: (1) proper error surfacing in output, (2) User-Agent string that complies with Wikipedia's policy (should include contact email), (3) fallback behavior when API is unavailable. Code architecture is good — the deep extraction pipeline (search -> details -> see_also) is well-designed.

benchmarks.raw_results_summary: Returned 0 results. arXiv API returned HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.
benchmarks.notes: arXiv API returned 500 error. Unlike Wikipedia, this method does surface the error in metadata.errors. The XML parsing code and field extraction logic look correct. The issue may be environmental (sandbox network restrictions) or a transient arXiv outage. The method uses HTTP (not HTTPS) for the arXiv API URL, which may cause issues with some proxies.

team_feedback.from_team2: The arXiv API call uses HTTP instead of HTTPS (http://export.arxiv.org) — should be upgraded to HTTPS. Error handling is better than Wikipedia method (errors appear in metadata). Needs retry logic with exponential backoff. The XML parsing code is well-structured. Consider adding a rate-limiting delay as arXiv requires 3-second delays between requests.

benchmarks.raw_results_summary: Returned 31 results, all from web search only. Wikipedia and arXiv sub-methods returned 0 results. Corroboration score was 1.0 across all results (no cross-referencing possible with only one active source).
benchmarks.notes: The hybrid method degrades gracefully when sub-methods fail, but effectively becomes DG-0001 when Wikipedia and arXiv are unavailable. The cross-referencing logic (keyword overlap scoring, URL matching) is well-designed but untestable until all sub-methods work. The corroboration scoring system is a good concept but needs all sources functional to provide value.

team_feedback.from_team2: The hybrid architecture is sound but currently operates as a degraded web-search-only method. Needs: (1) error reporting showing which sub-methods failed, (2) timeout configuration per sub-method, (3) ability to continue with partial results while flagging degraded mode. The cross-referencing and corroboration scoring is a strong concept that should be expanded.

method_quality_scores.notes: Clean code, good structure. Lacks rate limiting, retry logic, and error detail propagation. Output format is compliant with schema.
Well-architected code with deep extraction pipeline. Critical robustness failure: silently returns empty on HTTP errors. User-Agent non-compliant with Wikipedia policy.
Good XML parsing, proper namespace handling. Uses HTTP instead of HTTPS. Does surface errors in output. Lacks retry logic and rate limiting.
Good aggregation architecture. Graceful degradation works. Dynamic module loading is clever but fragile. Cross-referencing untestable with broken sub-methods.
